title: Hepatitis B immunization : introducing hepatitis B vaccine into national immunization services (العربية)

sections.title: Page 1

summary.text: The first page of the Arabic edition of the WHO note on introducing hepatitis B vaccine into national immunization services, describing hepatitis B as a major public health problem and stating that WHO recommends routine infant vaccination everywhere. It explains that the main aim is to prevent chronic infection and that immunizing all infants should be the top priority, with a birth dose to prevent mother-to-child transmission where perinatal infection is common, such as South-East Asia. The OCR text is partly garbled, with some figures and the header missing or corrupted.

sections.title: Page 2

summary.text: Discusses priorities where perinatal infection is less common, such as Africa, and notes that catch-up vaccination of older people is generally not advised where chronic infection is highly endemic but may be considered elsewhere, without Vaccine Fund support. It explains that monovalent vaccine must be used for the birth dose, outlines three schedule options linked to DTP doses, and describes giving the vaccine alongside other vaccines; the Arabic OCR contains some errors.

sections.title: Page 3

summary.text: Presents a table of options for adding hepatitis B vaccine to childhood immunization schedules with and without a birth dose, alongside other vaccines. It then covers injection equipment, recommending auto-disable syringes, and begins describing storage and shipping volumes; the table text is partly garbled in the OCR.

sections.title: Page 4

summary.text: Compares the packed volume of hepatitis B vaccine vials of different sizes with other routine vaccines and explains that the vaccine is stored at 2–8°C like DTP and must never be frozen. It also notes the need for safe use and disposal of safety boxes; the volume table is largely garbled in the extracted text.

sections.title: Page 5

summary.text: Answers practical questions on introducing hepatitis B vaccine, noting that prevalence data are usually sufficient to assess disease burden and discussing phased introduction and the choice between monovalent and combination vaccines. It covers using the introduction to strengthen immunization services and budgeting for capital and recurrent costs, and ends with the document number and copyright notice; parts of the OCR are garbled.
